subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Preparing and delivering a spoken presentation

questions.q: In the OCR GCSE English Language (J351) qualification, how does the Spoken Language Endorsement contribute to a candidate's grade?
options: It is reported as a separate grade (Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified) and does not count towards the 9–1 grade
It contributes 20% of the overall 9–1 grade
It contributes 40% of the overall 9–1 grade
It replaces the reading paper for weaker candidates
questions.explain: The endorsement is reported separately as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified and does not affect the numerical 9–1 grade.

questions.q: Which three components must a candidate complete for the Spoken Language Endorsement?
options: Give a presentation, respond to questions and feedback, and use spoken Standard English
Write an essay, read aloud, and give a presentation
Debate a partner, record a podcast, and answer an exam
Perform a drama piece, sit an oral exam, and take notes
questions.explain: Candidates must deliver a presentation, respond to questions and feedback, and demonstrate spoken Standard English.

questions.q: What is meant by 'spoken Standard English' in the context of the endorsement?
options: The widely accepted form of English using conventional grammar and vocabulary, appropriate to a formal audience
Speaking with a Received Pronunciation accent at all times
Using only complex, technical subject-specific terminology
Speaking as fast and fluently as possible without pausing
questions.explain: Standard English is the conventional grammar and vocabulary expected in formal contexts, not a particular accent.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of using spoken Standard English in the presentation?
options: Eliminating all trace of the candidate's regional accent
Using grammatically accurate sentence structures
Selecting vocabulary appropriate to a formal audience
Avoiding overly informal slang inappropriate to the context
questions.explain: Standard English concerns grammar and vocabulary, not accent, so candidates need not lose their regional accent.

questions.q: Who assesses the Spoken Language Endorsement?
options: The candidate's own teacher, who acts as assessor
An external OCR examiner who visits the school
Another candidate acting as a peer marker
An online automated speech-recognition system
questions.explain: The endorsement is teacher-assessed, with the teacher marking against the OCR criteria.

questions.q: During the 'listening and responding to questions' element, what is the candidate expected to do?
options: Listen to questions from the audience and respond appropriately and clearly
Ask the audience a series of prepared questions
Repeat the presentation a second time from memory
Remain silent while the teacher summarises their talk
questions.explain: Candidates must field questions and feedback from listeners and respond in a relevant, clear manner.

questions.q: On what topic may a candidate base their spoken presentation?
options: A topic they choose, which may be linked to their studies or a subject of personal interest
Only a set text from the English Literature specification
Only a current political news story chosen by the exam board
A topic randomly assigned by OCR on the day
questions.explain: Candidates select their own topic, which can relate to their studies or a personal interest.

questions.q: Why is planning and structuring the presentation important for a strong performance?
options: A clear structure helps the speaker sustain and develop ideas so the audience can follow the argument
It allows the candidate to read the whole talk word-for-word from a script
It guarantees a Distinction regardless of delivery
It removes the need to respond to any questions afterwards
questions.explain: A well-planned structure lets ideas be sustained and developed clearly for the audience.

questions.q: A candidate finishes their talk and an audience member asks a challenging question the candidate had not anticipated. Which response best meets the endorsement criteria?
options: Listen carefully, then answer relevantly and expand on their ideas using Standard English
Ignore the question and end the session
Say only 'I don't know' and sit down
Repeat a memorised section of the presentation unrelated to the question
questions.explain: Responding relevantly, listening well and developing ideas in Standard English demonstrates the assessed skills.

questions.q: Which of the following is a legitimate presentation format for the endorsement?
options: An individual talk, which may be followed by responding to questions
A written report submitted for moderation
A silent PowerPoint with no speaking
A group performance where the individual does not speak
questions.explain: The endorsement is centred on an individual spoken presentation followed by questions.

questions.q: A candidate says: 'We wasn't really bothered about them results, know what I mean?' during the formal presentation. Why might this weaken their spoken Standard English mark?
options: It uses non-standard grammar ('we wasn't') and informal filler unsuitable for a formal audience
It is too grammatically complex for the audience to follow
It uses vocabulary that is too formal and technical
It is spoken too clearly and precisely
questions.explain: 'We wasn't' is non-standard grammar and the filler is too informal for the required Standard English register.

questions.q: Which behaviour best demonstrates effective listening during the question phase?
options: Paying close attention to the question before giving a focused, relevant answer
Interrupting the questioner to give a rehearsed reply
Answering a different, easier question instead
Waiting in silence until the teacher moves on
questions.explain: Effective listening means attending fully to the question and then responding relevantly.

questions.q: How does the effective use of presentation techniques (such as tone, pace and emphasis) help a candidate?
options: They help engage the audience and convey meaning clearly and persuasively
They allow the candidate to speak in a monotone to appear serious
They are penalised because they distract from content
They replace the need for any structured content
questions.explain: Varying tone, pace and emphasis engages listeners and communicates meaning effectively.

questions.q: What grade outcomes are possible for the Spoken Language Endorsement?
options: Pass, Merit, Distinction, or Not Classified
Grades 1 to 9
A*, A, B, C, D, E, F, G
Pass or Fail only
questions.explain: The endorsement is graded Pass, Merit, Distinction, or Not Classified.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of spoken Standard English expected in the presentation?
options: Accurate and appropriate use of vocabulary and grammar
Frequent use of regional dialect words in place of standard terms
Consistent use of text-message abbreviations
Deliberate use of slang to sound relatable
questions.explain: Standard English requires accurate, appropriate vocabulary and grammatical accuracy.

questions.q: To achieve a higher (Distinction-level) performance when responding to questions, a candidate should aim to do what?
options: Respond fully and perceptively, developing and expanding their ideas in Standard English
Give the shortest possible one-word answers
Deflect every question back to the audience
Answer only questions they had pre-prepared answers for
questions.explain: Higher performances feature perceptive, developed responses expressed in Standard English.

questions.q: Why does OCR require the presentation to be delivered to an audience?
options: So the candidate can demonstrate the ability to engage and communicate with real listeners
Because a larger audience automatically raises the grade
So the audience can vote on the candidate's grade
Because presentations must always be filmed for OCR
questions.explain: An audience allows candidates to show genuine communication and engagement skills.

questions.q: A candidate has a strong regional accent but uses conventional grammar and formal vocabulary throughout. How should this be judged for spoken Standard English?
options: It can still meet the Standard English requirement, as accent is not assessed
It must be marked down because the accent is not neutral
It cannot be classified at all
It automatically achieves Distinction because of the accent
questions.explain: Standard English is about grammar and vocabulary, so a regional accent does not prevent meeting the requirement.

questions.q: In addition to questions, what else must a candidate respond to during this element of the endorsement?
options: Feedback from the audience
A written examination paper
A second candidate's presentation
A recorded set of OCR prompts
questions.explain: The criteria require candidates to listen and respond to both questions and feedback.

questions.q: Which of the following would best characterise a Distinction-level spoken presentation?
options: Ideas that are consistently sustained and developed with confident, effective delivery for the audience
A short talk read directly from cards with little audience awareness
A presentation that covers many topics briefly without developing any
A talk delivered entirely in informal, conversational language
questions.explain: Distinction performances sustain and develop ideas with confident, effective, audience-aware delivery.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Language (J351) specification; Non-exam Assessment: Spoken Language Endorsement
